# Viruses (disease agents smaller than bacteria) (`viruses`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: needs microorganisms, contagion_theory; helped by vaccines_attenuated, fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: A virus carries genetic material inside a protective coat. It can reproduce only by using the machinery of a living cell. Late nineteenth-century work on tobacco mosaic showed that an infectious agent could pass filters that retained ordinary bacteria. Filtration was evidence about the agent’s size; it could not by itself establish what the agent was. Most viruses are too small to resolve with a light microscope. Their dependence on host cells helps explain why antibacterial drugs do not treat viral disease and why prevention depends on the particular virus and its route of spread.
- Pitfalls:
  - Giving antibacterial drugs for virus diseases
  - Promising to show the germ of smallpox or influenza under the microscope
  - Trying to grow viruses on broth; they need living cells, eggs or animals
  - Using 'virus' in a period where the word simply means poison or any contagious matter
  - Blaming the 1918 influenza on Pfeiffer's bacillus, as most experts then did
- History: europe: 1884 – Chamberland's porcelain filter; 1892 Ivanovsky (St Petersburg) finds tobacco mosaic passes the filter; 1898 Beijerinck (Delft) concludes it is a new kind of agent; 1898 Loeffler and Frosch, foot-and-mouth disease; 1915–1917 Twort and d'Herelle find viruses of bacteria; 1933 human influenza virus isolated in London; 1939 first electron-microscope picture (Kausche, Pfankuch, Ruska); americas: 1901 – Reed's commission shows yellow fever is filterable; 1911 Rous's chicken tumour virus; 1931 Goodpasture grows viruses in hens' eggs; 1935 Stanley crystallises tobacco mosaic virus; 1949 Enders, Weller and Robbins demonstrate poliovirus growth in human tissue cultures
- Read:
  - Martinus W. Beijerinck, Ueber ein Contagium vivum fluidum als Ursache der Fleckenkrankheit der Tabaksblätter (1898)
  - A. P. Waterson and Lise Wilkinson, An Introduction to the History of Virology (1978)
  - Carl Zimmer, A Planet of Viruses (2011)
